title: The Woman in Black — Factual Accuracy Audit
author: Susan Hill
source_text: Susan Hill novel (1983), verified against LitCharts, Wikipedia, SuperSummary, Shmoop, RevisionWorld, SaveMyExams, and cross-checked chapter-by-chapter plot sources
text_note: All 15 lessons teach the Susan Hill NOVEL (1983), not the Stephen Mallatratt stage play adaptation. No play-specific staging or theatrical language was found. All boards correctly use novel-based content.

issues.location: Section 'The Ending: Stella and the Baby'
issues.claim: Then, on a beautiful sunny day at a park, Kipps sees the Woman in Black one last time. Moments later, the pony and trap carrying Stella and the baby crashes. Stella is killed. The baby dies in hospital.
issues.correct: Two errors here. (1) Location: the tragic ending takes place at a fair on the outskirts of London (described as a large park with a fairground), not simply 'a park'. The fair context is important — it is a place of innocent pleasure, which sharpens the horror. (2) Deaths: The novel's account is the reverse of the lesson's. The child is killed instantly in the accident; Stella survives the crash but lingers and dies from her injuries ten months later. The lesson states 'Stella is killed. The baby dies in hospital' — exactly the wrong way round. 'Baby dies in hospital' has no basis in the novel; it is the child who dies at the scene.
issues.source: LitCharts chapter 12 summary; SuperSummary; multiple GCSE study guides; novel ending chapter.

issues.claim: the pony and trap carrying Stella and their child is involved in an accident. Stella is killed; the child is killed.
issues.correct: In the novel the child is killed instantly in the crash; Stella survives the initial accident but dies from her injuries ten months later. Presenting both as killed simultaneously in the accident misrepresents the ending. The lesson's following quote — 'The pony swerved and bolted, the trap overturned... Stella and our son were thrown...' — is presented with ellipses as a direct quotation but appears to be a paraphrase; the exact phrasing 'our son' also implies Arthur named his child in the text, which the novel does not confirm (the child's name, Joseph, comes from the 2012 film adaptation, not the book).
issues.source: LitCharts chapter 12; SuperSummary; Wikipedia plot summary confirming child killed instantly, Stella dies ten months after.

issues.location: Section 'Nathaniel's Death: The Accident on the Causeway'
issues.claim: The child, the driver, and the horse were all drowned.
issues.correct: The victims of the causeway accident were Nathaniel, his nursemaid Rose Judd, and Keckwick's father (the driver). Three people died, not two. Omitting Rose Judd is a factual omission — her death certificate is found among Mrs Drablow's papers and forms part of the evidence Kipps uncovers. The horse dying is unconfirmed in the novel text; what matters is that three named people perished.
issues.source: LitCharts character notes on Keckwick; Shmoop analysis; multiple plot summaries confirming Rose Judd and Keckwick's father as named victims.

issues.location: Jennet backstory section and Key Fact box
issues.claim: In the Victorian period, an illegitimate child was a source of enormous shame... In Victorian society, illegitimacy was deeply shameful... The forced adoption reflects the harsh realities of Victorian society, where unmarried mothers had virtually no legal rights.
issues.correct: The novel is set in the Edwardian period (early 1900s), not the Victorian era (pre-1901). Hill deliberately writes an Edwardian ghost story. The lesson's own context lessons (Edexcel L01, Eduqas L01, Eduqas L02, Eduqas L04) all correctly identify the setting as Edwardian. Using 'Victorian' for Jennet's backstory is inconsistent with the novel's actual period setting and could mislead students in AO3 context responses. Edexcel L05 repeats the same error ('Victorian England', 'Victorian injustice'). These lessons should use 'Edwardian' throughout.
issues.source: Hill's own statements and multiple GCSE study guides confirming Edwardian setting. Eduqas lessons on same board correctly use 'Edwardian'.

issues.claim: She was an unmarried mother in Victorian England whose son Nathaniel was taken from her... She is a genuine victim of Victorian injustice: a woman stripped of her child by a patriarchal society...
issues.correct: As noted in WIB-004, the novel is set in the Edwardian period, not Victorian England. This lesson repeats the period error from L04. Both instances should read 'Edwardian England' and 'Edwardian injustice'. This matters for exam purposes as students may incorrectly cite Victorian social context when the relevant context is Edwardian.
issues.source: Consistent Edwardian setting throughout the novel; confirmed by multiple GCSE study resources.

issues.location: Section 'The Sound of the Pony and Trap'
issues.claim: the accident that killed Nathaniel Drablow
issues.correct: The boy is consistently referred to in the novel simply as 'Nathaniel'. While 'Drablow' is technically his adopted surname (he was adopted by Alice Drablow), the novel does not use 'Nathaniel Drablow' as a form of reference — he is always 'Nathaniel' or 'the child'. Using 'Nathaniel Drablow' is not incorrect but is an unusual usage not found in the source text, and could create unnecessary confusion with Mrs Alice Drablow. All other lessons in both boards refer to him correctly as 'Nathaniel'.
issues.source: LitCharts, RevisionWorld, and multiple study guides referring consistently to 'Nathaniel' without surname in lesson contexts.

clean_lessons.notes: Accurate. M.R. James dates (1862–1936) correct. Castle of Otranto (1764) correct. Turn of the Screw (1898) correct. Dickens Christmas Carol / Victorian ghost story tradition correct. Edwardian setting of novel correctly noted.

Accurate. Mrs Alice Drablow correct. Mr Bentley as employer not named here but Jerome as land agent correct. Funeral attendance (only Kipps and Jerome, plus the ghost) correct. Quote 'a tall woman, dressed in deepest black' with 'a wasted face' consistent with novel.

Accurate overall except WIB-006 (low). Nine Lives Causeway correctly named. Spider as Sam Daily's dog correct. Rocking chair in nursery correct. Pony and trap sound as spectral echo correct. 'Second visit' for Spider's introduction is plausible (Kipps crosses the causeway first without Spider, then takes her on subsequent visits).

Accurate. Retrospective first-person narration correctly described. Pathetic fallacy analysis sound. The observation that the ending takes place on a sunny day (subverting the weather pattern) is correct — the fair/park ending is indeed on a fine day. Nine Lives Causeway correctly referenced.

Accurate. Themes of fear, isolation, grief and revenge correctly presented. Quotes and key phrases ('They have learned to live with it', 'wasted face') used accurately. Sam Daily's role and Jerome's paralysis correctly described.

Accurate. Edwardian setting correctly identified. M.R. James's Ghost Stories of an Antiquary (1904) correct. Christmas Carol (1843) and The Signalman (1866) correct. Turn of the Screw (1898) correct. Bleak House fog reference is a reasonable teaching parallel (Dickens opens Bleak House with London fog). James's three-rule formula accurately described.

Accurate. Mr Bentley as Arthur's employer correct. Funeral attendance 'only Arthur and Mr Jerome' correct (the Woman in Black's presence is supernatural/spectral). Spider given to Arthur by Sam Daily correct. Quote 'a wasted face' with 'tautly stretched and thin' skin consistent with novel. Arthur described as 'young man, healthy, optimistic' correct.

Accurate. Nine Lives Causeway correctly named. House described as 'grey, tall, gaunt, like some bony old woman' — this quote is consistent with sources. Pony and trap sounds as spectral echo correct. Spider as Sam Daily's little terrier correct. Onomatopoeia 'sucking, churning' analysis sound.

Accurate. Edwardian setting correctly used throughout. Jennet's 'wasting disease' correctly named. Arthur's arc from rationalist to broken narrator correctly described. Sam Daily as bluff, practical landowner and 'reluctant ally' correct. Spider as terrier correct.

Accurate. Retrospective narration correctly described. Pathetic fallacy from 'raw and damp' London to 'desolate, grey, empty' marshes correct. Sound over sight as Hill's primary horror technique well-argued. Withholding technique accurately described.

Accurate. Marshes as symbol of hidden danger correct. Fog as obscuring truth and rational understanding correct. House/ghost fusion ('grey, tall, gaunt, like some bony old woman') correct. Locked nursery as forbidden knowledge and transgression correct. Rocking chair as absent motherhood symbol well-argued.

Accurate. Themes of fear, isolation, grief, revenge, innocence/guilt all correctly presented. Jennet's 'wasting disease' correct. Sam Daily's wife's 'premonitions' correctly referenced. Hill's departure from conventional ghost story resolution accurately noted.

cross_board_notes: Edexcel and Eduqas lessons share very similar content with minor board-appropriate variations. The two high-severity issues (ending deaths) appear in BOTH boards' L04 lessons, suggesting a shared source text error.
The Victorian/Edwardian period error (WIB-004, WIB-005) affects only the Edexcel lessons (L04, L05). The Eduqas lessons consistently and correctly use 'Edwardian' throughout.
No lesson from either board shows any evidence of confusion between the Susan Hill novel (1983) and the Stephen Mallatratt stage play adaptation. All content is novel-based.

Both boards correctly identify: 12 chapters, first-person retrospective frame narrative, Crythin Gifford as the town, Nine Lives Causeway, Eel Marsh House, Mrs Alice Drablow, Jennet Humfrye, Nathaniel, Sam Daily (Samuel Daily), Mr Jerome as land agent, Mr Bentley as Arthur's London employer, Spider as Sam Daily's terrier.

The novel's child's name (Arthur and Stella's baby): the novel does not name the child. 'Joseph' is from the 2012 film. Eduqas L04 uses 'our son' (from a paraphrased quote) which is acceptable. Edexcel L04 calls it 'the baby' which is correct.
